A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GDRO research, with matching authors, foundational definitions, algorithms, and proofs. The main text and all appendices are readable, and renamed or relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical results, proofs, and schematic illustrations, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes, including in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 Section 5 reports original experiments on a synthetic lower-bound environment and Adult income classification, including dominant-set trajectories, convergence comparisons, and group-sampling counts. Appendix F documents the experiments.

M1.justification: v2 introduces SB-GDRO-SA (Algorithm 9), which estimates the sparsity gap during optimization, halves lambda when dominant sets exceed a threshold, and refreshes samples subject to a lower cutoff. This is distinct from the retained SB-GDRO-Full, renamed SB-GDRO-A, and the existing dimension-free method moved to Appendix C.

E1.justification: v1 has no evaluated datasets or simulation scenarios. v2 adds actual simulation of the lower-bound construction and Adult income classification across ten race-by-gender groups. The theoretical construction already existed, but its empirical use is new.

E2.justification: v2 introduces an empirical baseline comparison against Zhang et al.'s Stochastic Mirror Descent for GDRO (SMD-GDRO), visibly reported against SB-GDRO-SA on Adult in Figure 3. v1 discusses prior algorithms theoretically but reports no evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The new experiments introduce protocols with 10^6 rounds, delta = 0.01, and target gaps of 0.005 for the synthetic instance and 0.001 for Adult. Section 5 and Appendix F specify normalized losses, single-sample updates, and a 10^7-round full-information procedure for estimating Adult's reference optimum.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses testing whether small dominant sets emerge during learning and how sampling concentrates across demographic groups. Figure 2 tracks dominant-set sizes and their running averages; Figure 4 examines Adult group-selection frequencies. v1 has no corresponding empirical diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports aggregation across five independent runs with seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. v1 has no empirical run information. The added reporting does not include confidence intervals, quantified dispersion, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds the first empirical findings. Figure 3 reports SB-GDRO-SA reaching an Adult optimality gap below 4 × 10^-5 before 400,000 samples, while SMD-GDRO remains near that gap around one million samples. Figures 2 and 4 additionally report small dominant sets and concentrated group sampling; these are new results, not improvements over measurements in v1.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix B.3 add the semi-adaptive sample-complexity theorem, its more general formulation, and supporting proofs. Appendix D also changes the regret term from K^(1-alpha)/(eta_T(1-alpha)) to (K^(1-alpha)-1)/(eta_T(1-alpha)), repairing the stated alpha-to-one limit used to obtain the Shannon-entropy bound.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add computationally efficient semi-adaptivity, a dimension-independent sample bound under a high-precision condition, and empirical claims of practicality and improved sample efficiency. v1's contributions were theoretical and left the computational expense of fully adaptive estimation unresolved.

C2.justification: v2 interprets convergence gains as overcoming initial estimation overhead by concentrating sampling on high-risk groups, and interprets disproportionate sampling of a small Adult subgroup as evidence of GDRO's robustness objective. It also explains the new method's high-precision restriction and explicitly qualifies suppression of log-log factors in Appendix B. The existing last-iterate-convergence limitation remains.

D1.justification: New Appendix F supplies substantial experimental reproduction information: synthetic loss scaling and parameters, Adult features and group composition, normalization by a common maximum feature norm, absence of batching, and the full-information reference-optimization procedure. These details accompany newly introduced experiments rather than disclose changed settings for an existing study.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same 29 works. v2 makes limited positioning refinements, including distinguishing bounded-loss assumptions in prior work, revising its description of prior sleeping-bandit tuning requirements, and explaining the suitability of SMD-GDRO as an empirical baseline.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: the generic optimization discussion moves into Appendix B.1, Section 4 is recast around full and semi-adaptivity, and the former dimension-free Section 5 moves to Appendix C. The introduction and explanations are rewritten, algorithms are renamed, and experimental discussion becomes a main section.

P2.justification: v2 adds three empirical figures showing dominant-set trajectories, convergence with a zoomed inset, and group-selection counts. Table 1 gains the semi-adaptive bound, a new algorithm display is added, and MaxP moves into the main text. The original lower-bound illustration is retained as Figure 5.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by partly addressing v1's explicit computational-practicality limitation through SB-GDRO-SA, correcting the entropy-limit proof step, and adding the first empirical tests with documented settings. The new guarantee is conditional on high precision, and empirical support remains limited to two instances without uncertainty intervals. Nevertheless, the gains in theoretical support and demonstrated applicability are substantial.
